definition.text: The study of the minerals in soil, one of the branches, with soil physics, chemistry and biology, through which soil processes are studied quantitatively.

facts.text: Most of the elements plants need come from the chemical breakdown of soil minerals.
As roots remove nutrients from the soil solution, weathering of soil minerals helps replenish them, along with ion exchange and decay of organic matter.
Soil colour is mainly influenced by soil mineralogy.
Gypsum, calcite, feldspar or quartz grains can be clay-sized without behaving like true clay minerals.
Soil minerals retain phosphorus, by adsorption onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides in acid soils and precipitation onto calcite in neutral to calcareous ones.
Organic matter binds to soil minerals: hydrophobic molecules partition onto them and stay longer in soil, and particulate organic matter adheres to them.
Weathering of soil minerals releases salts, which drainage flushes out or evaporation concentrates near the surface.
Advances in soil mineralogy, with the other soil sciences, have added new tools to the study of soil formation.

definition.text: Carbonate that forms in place within a soil, as opposed to carbonate inherited from the bedrock or parent material.

facts.text: Acid hydrolysis by dissolved carbon dioxide, called carbonation, can weather primary minerals into secondary carbonate minerals.
Horizon descriptions in the WRB and the FAO guidelines mark accumulated secondary carbonates with the suffix k.
Secondary carbonates define WRB groups: Calcisols accumulate them, Chernozems and Kastanozems have them, Phaeozems lack them within one metre.
Carbon isotopes in pedogenic carbonate nodules of paleosols are used to reconstruct past atmospheric carbon dioxide.
It can form during soil wetting and drying, which underlies proposed proxies for past seasonality.

definition.text: The sequence in which common silicate minerals crystallize from a cooling basaltic magma, summarized by the petrologist Norman L. Bowen.

facts.text: Olivine and calcium plagioclase crystallize first, followed by pyroxene, amphibole, biotite, sodium plagioclase, orthoclase, muscovite and finally quartz.
It has a continuous branch of feldspars that grow more sodium-rich as temperature falls, and a discontinuous branch of mafic minerals.
Bowen derived it in the early 1900s by melting powdered rock and noting the minerals that formed at progressively cooler temperatures.
It explains why some minerals tend to occur together and others almost never do.
Because minerals are most stable near their conditions of formation, the series also ranks resistance to weathering at Earth's surface, with the last-formed most stable.

title: Goldich dissolution series

definition.text: A ranking of how fast common igneous minerals weather at Earth's surface, with minerals formed at higher temperatures and pressures less stable than those formed at lower ones.

facts.text: S. S. Goldich derived it in 1938 after studying soil profiles and their parent rocks.
Mafic minerals, rich in iron and magnesium, are less stable than felsic, silica-rich ones; the order echoes Bowen's reaction series.
Apatite is the quickest common igneous mineral to weather and quartz the slowest, a difference that can span millions of years.
Quartz, least prone to weathering, is very common as a residual mineral in residual soils, while basaltic minerals weather relatively quickly.
It covers intrinsic mineral properties; extrinsic factors such as climate, through water-to-rock ratio, pH and alkalinity, also control weathering rate.
Mafic rocks weather to serpentine, Mg- and Ca-rich clays and iron oxides; felsic rocks to clays such as kaolinite, montmorillonite and illite.
It is applied to lithosequences, soils compared under similar weathering conditions so that differences reflect their parent minerals.
Experiments by White and Brantley (2003) found K-feldspar and plagioclase weather at similar rates, so the series may not hold for all weathering processes.

definition.text: A technique that uses X-ray, neutron or electron diffraction on powdered or microcrystalline samples to characterize the structure of materials.

facts.text: Each crystalline solid gives a distinctive pattern; line positions, set by lattice spacings, and their intensities act as a fingerprint.
A mixture such as a soil sample shows several superposed patterns, from which the relative amounts of each phase can be found.
Diffraction occurs when radiation with a wavelength comparable to atomic spacings reflects off planes of atoms and interferes constructively.
Bragg's law, nλ = 2d sin θ, links the wavelength λ, the lattice spacing d and the glancing angle θ; the Braggs proposed it in 1913.
It has long been used to identify and classify minerals, and works on nearly any material for which a reference pattern exists.
The 2021 Powder Diffraction File held over 1,047,661 reference materials.
Its strengths are simple sample preparation and fast measurement; it mainly identifies phases rather than solving unknown structures.

definition.text: The emission of characteristic X-rays from a material excited by high-energy X-rays or gamma rays, whose energies and intensities reveal which elements are present and in what amounts.

facts.text: It is a non-destructive technique for elemental analysis used in geochemistry, archaeology and forensic science, among other fields.
Minerals may be ground and pressed into a tablet or, for accurate work, dissolved in borate glass and cast into a bead.
In pressed mineral powders the finer minerals gather at the surface and mixtures cause absorption effects that depart from theory.
XRF tools are increasingly run with cone penetration test probes for in situ soil measurements.

definition.text: A technique that records the infrared absorption or emission spectrum of a solid, liquid or gas over a wide range of wavelengths at once.

facts.text: A mathematical Fourier transform converts the raw data into the spectrum, which gives the method its name.
Geologists use it to quantify water and carbon dioxide in minerals and glasses.
Allophane, which lacks long-range order, is identified by its distinctive infrared spectrum and X-ray diffraction pattern.
Infrared spectroscopy is among the methods, with X-ray and electron diffraction, used to study clay minerals.

definition.text: A technique that bombards small volumes of a solid with an electron beam and reads the emitted X-rays to determine its chemical composition non-destructively.

facts.text: It shares its principle with the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy of scanning electron microscopes, but uses a fixed beam and aims at analysis rather than imaging.
It is used mostly by mineralogists and petrologists, revealing chemical zoning from core to rim of a mineral grain that records its history.
Tephrochronology relies on geochemical fingerprinting of ash, usually with an electron microprobe.
Wavelength-dispersive analysis is limited for light elements such as hydrogen, lithium and beryllium.

definition.text: The study of how climate, sediment transport, pollution and other environmental influences affect magnetic minerals, using their magnetic properties as proxies.

facts.text: The main magnetic minerals are iron oxides such as magnetite, maghemite and hematite, and iron sulfides such as greigite and pyrrhotite.
Magnetic susceptibility and remanence are used to estimate mineral size and composition; measurements are quick and non-invasive.
Susceptibility profiles of alternating loess and paleosols in north-central China mapped Quaternary monsoon variations.
Soil magnetism rises when goethite and ferrihydrite are converted to maghemite by heat.

definition.text: A mineral denser than 2.9 g/cm3, usually one of the dense minor components of siliciclastic sediments.

facts.text: Common heavy minerals include zircon, tourmaline, rutile, garnet and magnetite, dense minerals that resist weathering.
The relative proportions of heavy minerals, a heavy mineral suite, help reveal the provenance of sediments.
Being minor constituents, they are separated for study in a dense liquid such as bromoform, in a funnel or centrifuge.
Deep weathering concentrates heavy minerals in residual accumulations.

title: Selective extraction of iron oxides

definition.text: Chemical extractions used in soil analysis to dissolve particular iron- and aluminium-bearing mineral phases selectively so they can be measured.

facts.text: Acid ammonium oxalate, at pH 3, extracts iron and aluminium from poorly crystalline minerals such as ferrihydrite, from iron(II) minerals such as magnetite, and from organic matter.
Dithionite with a complexing agent such as citric acid reduces iron(III) oxyhydroxides to soluble iron(II) and removes amorphous iron(III) phases.
Dithionite is a reducing agent with a reduction potential of −0.66 V at pH 7.

notes: Concept passes test 5: described on the Ammonium oxalate and Dithionite pages; neither page warrants its own entry.

definition.text: A hydrous manganese dioxide mineral, nominally MnO2·nH2O, the main manganese mineral at Earth's surface.

facts.text: It occurs as fine-grained, poorly crystalline aggregates in soils, sediments, rock coatings such as desert varnish and marine nodules.
Most natural birnessite is thought to be made by microorganisms, since biological oxidation of Mn(II) is faster than abiotic oxidation.
Vacancies in its layers are balanced by interlayer cations such as calcium, copper, zinc, lead and cadmium.
Manganese oxides can oxidize trivalent chromium in soils to hexavalent chromium.

definition.text: A green iron potassium phyllosilicate of the mica group, very friable and with very low resistance to weathering.

facts.text: It forms in place in marine settings, commonly under low oxygen, and indicates continental shelf deposits laid down slowly.
As the main component of greensand it is a common potassium source in fertilizers and is used to adjust soil pH.
Greensand is low in potassium, so it pays to transport it only short distances to fields.
Konstantin Glinka's 1896 master's thesis dealt with glauconite's origin, composition and weathering.

title: Jarosite

definition.text: A basic hydrous sulfate of potassium and ferric iron, KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, formed by the oxidation of iron sulfides.

facts.text: It is common in acid mine drainage and acid sulfate soil environments.
When it forms from pyrite oxidation in clays, its potassium comes mainly from illite or K-feldspar.
With schwertmannite it holds retained acidity, releasing it slowly through hydrolysis of Fe3+ and Al3+; the WRB horizon suffix j marks their accumulation.
Rovers have found it on Mars, a sign of strongly oxidizing surface conditions.

related: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils

definition.text: An iron oxyhydroxysulfate mineral, ideally Fe8O8(OH)6(SO4)·nH2O, usually seen as brownish-yellow crusts.

facts.text: It forms in iron-rich, acidic sulfate waters with a pH of 2 to 4.
It is commonly an orange precipitate in streams and lakes affected by acid mine drainage.
It is central to iron-sulfur geochemistry in the acid sulfate soils of coastal lowlands.
First described in 1994, it is named for the soil scientist Udo Schwertmann of the Technical University of Munich.

definition.text: A group of microporous, crystalline aluminosilicate minerals widely used as adsorbents and catalysts.

facts.text: Their negatively charged aluminium centres need accompanying cations, which can be exchanged, giving zeolites ion-exchange properties.
Over 40 naturally occurring frameworks are known among 253 identified by December 2018.
Altered volcanic glass has formed zeolite deposits.
Much material sold as zeolite is ground volcanic tuff holding little zeolite, used for building stone, aggregate, cement and soil conditioners.

definition.text: The amorphous, non-crystalline product of rapidly cooled magma.

facts.text: Lacking a crystal structure, it reacts easily with water and breaks down over time, forming new minerals.
Allophane forms by weathering of volcanic glass and feldspars, and devitrified glass in ash beds becomes bentonite clay.
Vitric Andosols, with limited soil formation, still contain much volcanic glass.
Soils with duripans are often found in volcanic areas and show evidence of ash or volcanic glass.
